The Required Measurements for the Myrtle and Willow, 2 Seifim: The minimum
size for myrtle and willow is three tefachim. For the spine of the lulav, it is four tefachim, such that the spine of the lulav extends one tefach beyond the myrtle. [The tefach we are talking about can be gotten by] taking an amah of five tefachim and dividing it into six, using three for the myrtle. The measure of the myrtle and willow ends up being 2.5 [normal] tefachim,' which is ten godels. The measure of the spine of the lulav is thirteen and a third godels. There is one who says that the minimum size of the lulav spine is fourteen godels. And there are those who say that the minimum size of the myrtle and willow is twelve godels and the minimum size of the lulav spine is sixteen godels((and we do this, initially).):

eliyah_rabbah.en: [1] And so is the practice, etc. The Bach rules this way as a matter of law. The Shelah wrote: Even Shoev wrote that the face of the lulav should be toward him and the spine outward, but in Tolaas Yaakov he wrote the opposite, and the secret is "you shall see My back, but My face shall not be seen." Since the author of Tolaas Yaakov was a great master of the wisdom of Kabbalah, it is proper to practice like him, end quote. This is how the world practices. But in Eliyahu Zuta I wrote that the primary view is like Even Shoev, for I saw in the Darkei Moshe and Mateh Moshe that they agreed with him. So too wrote Abudraham, Rabbeinu Saadiah Gaon, and Shiltei Gibborim in the name of Sefer Eshkol. The Maharik and the Shelah did not see the agreement of the Geonim mentioned above. One should also add what the Beis Yosef wrote at the end of siman 645, that its face is the side of the spine and its back is the other side. If so, even according to the secret of "you shall see My back," etc., the spine must be outward. However, I found in Shibbolei HaLeket, siman 118, this language: and in the bundle, the spine of the lulav must be opposite the heart. Mateh Moshe and the later authorities wrote that one should bind the aravah on the left, the hadas on the right, and the lulav in the middle. What is written in the writings of the Arizal, to bind three hadasim and aravos, I have not seen anyone practice this way.

turei_zahav.en: The measure of the hadas, etc. The dispute among the opinions in this matter is as follows. It is stated in the Gemara: the measure of a hadas and aravah is three tefachim. Rabbi Tarfon says: with an amah of five tefachim. Shmuel said: the law is like Rabbi Tarfon. We explain that statement of Rabbi Tarfon as follows: take before you an amah of five tefachim, divide them into six, take from them three for the hadas, and the rest for the lulav. How much is this? Two and a half. Rashi explained: take for yourself an amah of five average tefachim and divide it into six parts of small tefachim, and with them the measure is three for the hadas and aravah and four for the lulav. Rabbi Tarfon is being lenient, and this is what Rabbi Tarfon says to the first Tanna: those three tefachim by which we measure, and ordinary three tefachim are half an amah, should be small tefachim, and should be only half an amah within an amah of five tefachim. We challenge this: if so, these three tefachim are only two and a half average tefachim, for each small tefach is one sixth less than an average tefach; but did Shmuel not say three average tefachim? The answer is that Shmuel was not precise, in the stringent direction, and gave a larger measure. There are opinions about this regarding the fourth tefach of the lulav. The first opinion holds that this tefach too is a small tefach, one sixth less than an average tefach. Each tefach is four thumbs, so the two and a half tefachim of the hadas are ten thumbs, and the fourth tefach, which is also small, contains three thumbs and one third of a thumb. Its sign is 13 thirds, meaning thirteen thirds. The middle opinion holds that specifically the three tefachim of the hadas are small, namely ten thumbs, but the fourth tefach of the lulav is large, like the ordinary average tefach, namely four thumbs. It follows that the total is fourteen thumbs. The third opinion holds that the law is not like Shmuel, who ruled like Rabbi Tarfon, but we maintain like the first Tanna, who holds that all four tefachim are specifically average. It follows that all together there are sixteen thumbs. Even Shoev wrote that one should bind the aravah on the left, the hadas on the right, and the lulav in the middle, and there is a secret in this. It is written in Tolaas Yaakov that there is one who takes the spine of the lulav toward his face and the face of the lulav outward, in the manner of "you shall see My back," etc.
